newsitem.title: EGYPT: Cairo court jails collapsed block owner seven years.
newsitem.headline: Cairo court jails collapsed block owner seven years.

text.p: An Egyptian court passed a seven-year prison sentence on Wednesday on the owner of a Cairo apartment block which collapsed in a pile of rubble last October killing 64 people and injuring 16.

The landlord, Raouf Ibrahim Wissa, was convicted of manslaughter and causing injury. Two engineers who were remodelling one of the flats, Ahmed Riyad and Ashraf el-Naggari, received three-year sentences on the same charges.

The collapse of the 13-storey building, in the northern suburb of Heliopolis, was the deadliest of its kind since the Cairo earthquake of 1992. Rescue workers flew in from Japan and Germany to help in the long search for survivors.
But Judge Mohamed Ahmed Abu Zeid, ruling in a state security court, dropped all charges related to the construction work.
Wissa had also been charged with disregarding the design plans, constructing faulty supports and adding five illegal floors on top of the building.
The two engineers were fined 325,000 pounds ($98,000) each and will be struck off the register of contractors and engineers for one year, Abu Zeid added.
The state security court acquitted Abdel Aziz Khodeir, secretary general of the Association of Egyptian Banks, which had contracted the engineers to remodel the first-floor flat.

The verdict said: "The main reason for the collapse was that the weight exceeded the design weight after the number of floors was increased...and that the supporting pillar was removed in the flat of the Association of Banks."

Lawyers and relatives of the three defendants disputed the verdict. "It is a very strange sentence. The court acquitted Wissa of all construction-related charges," said Wissa's lawyer Osama Mahmoud Abul Nil. "How can a defendant be convicted with the outcome of the actions of which he was acquitted?"
Naggary's lawyer, Naeem Fouad Wahba, said hostile public opinion had played a part. "Sixty million Egyptians have heared of the case. So how could a defendant in such a case be acquitted?" he said.
But the verdict explained that Wissa had been convicted of building without a licence and fined five pounds ($1.5). It is unlawful to try a defendant twice on the same charge, it added.
There is no appeal against verdicts by state securtiy courts. But the defence lawyers said they would send pleas for leniency to the deputy military governor, who is Prime Minister Kamal Ganzouri.
"This is injustice, you infidels," Riyad's wife cried after hearing the verdict.
"It is an unfair sentence. What did Raouf do? He was just working hard," said Wissa's brother Andrew.

Mervat Abdul Aziz Mahmoud, an engineer who said she had no connection with those involved in the case, said the blame lay elsewhere. "All the defendants should be acquitted. The real responsibility lies with the local council," she said.
Investigations after the collapse of the building showed that the local authorities have failed to enforce building regulations in hundreds of cases across Cairo.
The government reacted to public outrage by introducing mandatory jail sentences for people who add extra floors or renovate a building in violation of the regulations.
